The test image shows a soybean stem being examined at the soil line, with clear reddish-brown to dark brown discoloration/lesions on the lower stem/hypocotyl area. This points to a soil-borne/root/stem disease. Top candidates: **Phytophthora**, **Rhizoctonia**, **Fusarium**, **Pythium_damping_off**.

Let me view reference images for these candidates in parallel.

The Rhizoctonia reference image (bottom-left panel) shows an almost identical scenario — hand holding stem at soil line with reddish-brown discoloration. This is a strong match. Let me view more references to confirm and rule out alternatives.

**Analysis Summary:**

- **Test image**: A thin soybean stem/hypocotyl being held at soil line, showing a **reddish-brown to orange-brown discoloration** on the lower stem with dark spots, on dark moist soil.

**Comparison:**
- **Rhizoctonia**: Reference bottom-left panel is nearly **identical** — hand holding thin stem at soil line with the same reddish-brown coloring. Description: "reddish-brown lesions on the hypocotyls at the soil line that are sunken and remain firm and dry." ✅ Strong match.
- **Phytophthora**: Shows darker brown lesion extending up from taproot, more advanced wilting/damping off. The test image color is more reddish/orange, not the darker chocolate-brown of Phytophthora. ❌ Weaker.
- **Fusarium**: Shows more extensive black/dark root decay with lateral root loss. ❌ Different.
- **Pythium**: Young seedlings with soft, water-soaked rot — much younger plants, soft tissue. ❌ Different.
- **Charcoal_Rot**: Distinctly gray/silver coloration. ❌ Different color entirely.
- **Brown_Stem_Rot / Sudden_death_syndrome**: Internal pith symptoms, older plants, foliar necrosis. ❌ Different.

The reddish-brown, firm, dry lesion at the soil line on a young stem closely matches **Rhizoctonia** both visually and symptomatically.

This matches the diagnostic description of 'reddish-brown, sunken, firm and dry lesions on hypocotyls at the soil line.' Phytophthora was considered but shows a darker chocolate-brown lesion typically extending higher up the stem."}
